History:
- Chief complaint: Chest tightness for ~3 hours.
- Associated symptoms: Mild shortness of breath (not at rest; worse with stairs), wheeze, dry cough (non-productive). No chest pain (tightness rather than pain).
- Recent illness: Had a cold last week with sore throat and runny nose; upper respiratory symptoms now improved except persistent cough.
- Triggers/context: Ran out of inhalers about a week ago and has not used them since; history of hay fever and dust allergies.
- Prior episodes: Severe asthma exacerbation in high school requiring hospital admission and intubation; otherwise no recent severe attacks.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Allergic rhinitis/hay fever; dust allergy.
- Childhood eczema; childhood milk protein allergy.
- Family history: Mother with eczema; father with asthma.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented. Ran out ~1 week ago.
  - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented. Ran out ~1 week ago.
  - Spacer previously owned; not routinely used.

Physical Examination:
- Telehealth visit; no vitals or peak flow obtained.
- Patient reports: No shortness of breath at rest; increased breathlessness with stairs. No chest pain; chest tightness present. Dry cough. Wheeze reported.

Impression:
- Acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by recent viral upper respiratory infection and lapse in controller/rescue inhaler use.

Management Plan:
- Prescriptions:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Spacer device with usage instructions.
  - Short course of oral steroids: 2 tablets each morning for 5 days (drug name and dose not documented).
- Inhaler use:
  - Resume daily Clenil once improved (morning use as advised).
  - Use Ventolin as needed for wheeze.
  - Use spacer to improve inhaler delivery.
- Safety-netting:
  - Seek medical attention if needing Ventolin more than every 3 hours, or if worsening shortness of breath, chest tightness/pain, or light-headedness.
- Work/activity:
  - Rest advised; may self-certify off work up to 7 days.
- Logistics:
  - Prescriptions to be sent; expected availability within ~1 hour per clinician.

Patient Summary:
- 26-year-old with asthma presents with 3 hours of chest tightness, wheeze, and dry cough after a recent cold and a week without inhalers. No shortness of breath at rest; exertional symptoms present.
- Clinical picture consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation. Plan includes restarting inhalers with a spacer, a short steroid course, rest, and clear safety-net instructions.

Key Takeaways:
- Start oral steroids as prescribed and restart inhalers with spacer use.
- Use Ventolin as needed; if needed more often than every 3 hours, seek medical care.
- Seek urgent care if symptoms worsen (increasing breathlessness, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness).

Next Steps:
- Obtain and start the prescribed inhalers, spacer, and oral steroid course today.
- Monitor symptoms closely; follow the safety-net advice.
- No tests or scheduled follow-up documented; seek medical review if symptoms do not improve or worsen.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals, peak flow, oxygen saturation, lung exam, or objective respiratory assessment; medication doses/strengths and steroid drug name/dose not documented; smoking status and vaccination history not discussed; no formal asthma action plan documented.
- Internal conflicts: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief audio dropouts during discussion of steroid side effects.
